title: Topological insulators on complex networks
authors: Sunkyu Yu, Xianji Piao, Namkyoo Park
abstract: The landscape of topological insulators has expanded beyond its traditional domain of periodic lattices with short-range hopping. Related studies have explored topological phenomena under non-Euclidean geometries, disordered structures, and long-range hopping, progressively narrowing the gap between topological phases of matter and complex networks. Here we demonstrate that genuine complex networks, far beyond periodic lattices and their conventional variants, can themselves host topological insulating phases. By developing a nonconflicting design framework for multiple topological objectives, we realize topological insulators in high-degree Hofstadter lattices and across regular, small-world, and random networks. This generalization uncovers distinct network-specific features, including an expanded range of attainable topological characteristics, a degree-dependent transition from Hofstadter-type to Haldane-type Chern insulators, and, most notably, the superior robustness and reconfigurability of small-world topological insulators. Our graph-theoretic framework establishes network complexity as a resource for realizing high-capacity and reconfigurable topological insulators.
summary: This paper proves that topological insulating phases can be engineered on arbitrary complex networks, moving beyond simple periodic lattices. By developing a sophisticated design framework, the authors show that network structure, especially small-world characteristics, enhances topological robustness and directional transport. This establishes network complexity as a key resource for realizing advanced quantum electronic functionalities.
main_problem: The research aims to generalize the concept of topological insulators beyond simple periodic lattices to complex, arbitrary network structures.
main_result: The study demonstrates that complex networks, particularly small-world architectures, can host robust topological insulating phases, with network complexity acting as a resource for high-capacity and reconfigurable transport.
method: A gradient-based, conflict-free multi-objective inverse-design framework is developed to tailor hopping phases and node positions to achieve desired topological invariants.
model_or_system: The system models topological insulators on complex graphs, including high-degree Hofstadter lattices, regular, small-world, and random networks, governed by a generalized magnetic graph Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Local Chern index ($C_L$), local gap ($\mu_L$), chirality ($\eta$), and port-to-port transmission matrices ($T_{pq}$).
important_parameters: Node degree ($k$), rewiring parameter ($ho$), and energy ($E$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on 2D embedding of abstract networks and uses spectral localizers and surrogate models for optimization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the design process, the evolution of topological phases across network topologies (regular to random), and the superior circulator behavior and robustness of small-world TIs.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops a design framework, applies it to various network types (Hofstadter, small-world, random), and analyzes the resulting topological invariants, robustness against disorder, and directional transport properties.
why_interesting: The focus on network topology and disorder robustness connects directly to understanding complex quantum systems, which is relevant for designing quantum devices or modeling quantum information flow in structured media.
